description: Great ideas come from diverse perspectives! We are building a dynamic team to tackle the 2026 Space Apps Challenge through creative design, effective communication, and tech innovation. Whether you bring skills in graphic design, writing, research, or coding, you'll have a role here. Join our team and let's turn space data into meaningful stories and tools!
summary:
Nitro Gravity: Build it. Launch it. Learn precisely why.

Space missions rarely fail for one reason. Gravity, drag, mass, power, structure and budget all pull against each other. Nitro Gravity, built by Team Nitro Gravity in Chennai for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Space Mission Design Game), lets you feel that balance in real time.
What we built: players choose Earth, the Moon or Mars, each with its own gravity, air density and sky. They build a rocket from parts and structure materials, launch it in a 3D scene, and get a debrief naming exactly why it succeeded or failed.
Real engineering constraints. Four rules decide every mission: thrust-to-weight of at least 1.2, budget friendly, mass of 5,000 kg or less, and net power above zero. A liftoff load above 3 g breaks plain aluminium, so stronger materials cost and weigh more. One change moves several limits at once, so every choice is a trade-off.

Learning that sticks: each debrief is a specific lesson, so you know which rule failed and what to change next.

Trusted foundation: the physics (thrust, mass flow, gravity, drag) sits in its own module, checked by three reference builds: a crash, a success, and a design that fails on power and budget. Earth’s radius and gravity match NASA fact sheets; NASA Glenn thrust and mass-flow relationships guide the model.
Accessible: a cinematic 3D scene with a detailed rocket and launch tower, in any browser with no account or install, supporting quality education (SDG 4).
details:
What it does and how it works

Nitro Gravity is a browser game about the physics of building and launching rockets. It's mission-design, 3D, everything's in your browser. Select your planet, your gravity, and your atmosphere, and then design your rocket to fit your budget using parts and structure materials; launch it in a cinematic 3D scene; and get a debrief telling you exactly why it either succeeded or failed. Four simple rules determine everything:

Thrust-to-weight ratio of minimum 1.2

a budget of $1.0M or less

Mass of 5,000 kg or less

Net power above zero

Plain aluminium needs to be broken with a below 3 g liftoff load. Therefore, other materials must be used and these increase the cost and weight of a rocket. The simulation applies thrust, mass flow, gravity and drag.

Impacts and benefits

Players can even see a single tweak affect multiple constraints, which is the reality of spaceflight design. Every debriefing is a lesson, so each launch makes the next one smarter. It requires no account or installation, so any student with the link can participate. Our goal is to make spaceflight engineering accessible and to foster quality education (SDG 4).

NASA and space-related

This Moon tab is tied to the real world. NASA's Artemis II was the first crewed Artemis launch, the first human lunar mission in over 50 years, and the first lunar flyby in nearly a decade, with a close flyby of the Moon in April 2026. It launched on 1 April 2026 from Launch Pad 39B at the Kennedy Space Centre. Our Moon destination lets you take on the challenge that the Artemis mission team solved.

foxweather

Gravity changes the design. NASA's fact sheets give surface gravity as 1.62 m/s² for the Moon and 3.73 m/s² for Mars, and 9.81 m/s² on Earth. The same rocket has roughly six times the thrust-to-weight ratio on the Moon and about 2.6 times on Mars, so a design must be tuned to its world. Players find out by playing.

Constants. The radius of Earth and a standard gravity are both as defined by NASA's Earth Fact Sheet.

Science in action! NASA Glenn Research Centre's education pages work out that the thrust ratio: Thrust = mass flow x exhaust velocity – no outside air needed! That's why rockets fly in a vacuum. They also show us what the special power of space engines is – specific impulse.

The same process as real missions. NASA Systems Engineering Handbook (SP-2016-6105 Rev 2) takes us on the journey from mission concept, requirements and design. Our own loop of destination, constraints, build, and review has taken the same journey.

NASA also teaches. NASA Glenn's Rocket Modeller is a design-then-launch simulator for learners.

Designed for the challenge. NASA's 2026 Space Apps announcement states that some challenges require mission design trade-offs. Our rules create precisely those trade-offs.

Tools used

JavaScript, HTML, and CSS

Three.js r128 for 3D

Python for the build script

Testing with Node.js

Inter typography

Vercel for hosting and GitHub for code

No special hardware beyond a modern browser

How it is creative

The debrief elucidates why, not just fail or succeed.

Contradictory rules create a constant compromise in each decision.

One engineering problem changes across three worlds.

The scene is ready with a detailed rocket with an ogive nose, bell engines, grid fins and segmented solar wings, on a pad with a lattice tower, floodlights, glow from exhaust and image-based reflections.

Factors the team looked at

Accuracy: constants compared with NASA fact sheets.

Accessibility: a static site with no sign-in.

Learning value: immediate, specific feedback.

Reliability: the physics is isolated in its own module and is validated by three reference builds (a crash, a success, and a design that fails on power and budget).

Realism: limits of budget, mass, power and structure combined.
